notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa014b.opp-l: Line 1: the edition numbers the section of Chapter II as '5' and Chapter III as '4'; read as 3 and 4. 'tillgentia' read as 'fulgentia' (gleaming); 'signili' as the truncated 'significat'. 'Jesus' in Chapters II and IV is Joshua (the Latin uses the same name; the text plays on it meaning 'Saviour'). Line 4: the Hermetic quotations (from the Latin Asclepius tradition) are obscure, especially 'Est autem. Quis? Filii inenarrabilis sermo sapientiae sanctus sanctus', rendered tentatively. 'adversario-' read as 'adversarios'. Line 5: the bracketed sentence '[Et homo est, inquit, et quis cognoscet eum?]' is garbled in the scan ('tIt', 'quia', 'a ?'); it appears to echo Jer. 17:9 and is marked by the edition as doubtful. 'Quis es Domine?' at Exod. 3:4 differs from the Vulgate. The sentence and the John reference (8:25) continue into the next stretch.
Line 7: 'natus est humo' read as 'natus est homo' (born a man). 'Latens magnus' is terse; rendered literally as 'hidden [as] great'. Scripture references follow the edition's (Vulgate) numbering.

Many scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'ainis' = aliis, 'frodo' = modo, 'aquis' = inquis, 'tuque … me ipse' = usque … erit iste, 'sanctor,' = sanctae, 'bominum' = Dominum, 'Fine' = sine, 'IV iri' = Patri, 'rxore' = ex ore, 'Λέγος' = Λόγος, 'Detis' = Deus). A printed footnote ('Quidam Mss., mundo') embedded in line 1 is omitted. In the Solomon passage the text 'ne unum vivum, ne undecumque conceptum, jamque parturo' is garbled; read as 'ne unum vivum, undecumque conceptum, jamque partum, perderet'. 'calciare velle aeternitatem' is uncertain: read as 'calcare' ('trample on'); 'calculare' ('reckon') is also possible. Line 9: the Isaiah 45:1 quotation reads 'Christo meo Domino' ('to my Christ the Lord'), where the Vulgate has 'Christo meo Cyro' ('to my anointed, Cyrus'); translated as the text gives it. Several scripture references are misprinted in the edition (e.g. Isa. 45:4 for 45:1, Matt. 27:4 for 17:4, John 8:46 for 8:42); corrected silently in the references. Line 8: 'Non illis ortus qui non est' is awkward and possibly corrupt; rendered literally.

Line 9: stray footnote marks (nubila tonant3, divinitatem4, doctorem 1 dedisti 2, speluncam (a), paganum (6), mimicum 1) omitted. 'Deus Virtus' rendered 'God the Power'; perhaps for 'Deus virtutum' (God of hosts). 'non mimicum aliquid' rendered 'nothing theatrical'; 'mimicum' may be a misprint for 'inimicum' (nothing hostile [to this]). 'exsufflas' refers to the exorcistic breathing used in Arian rebaptism. Scripture references corrected where evidently misscanned: John 13:10, 10:30, Jer. 49:16, Ps. 33:9, Matt. 3:17. Line 11: chapter and book numbers read where misscanned (cap. 18 for 48, book 1 for 'f', cap. 11 for 'it', cap. 11 for 'ii', chs. 3 and 4 for '5 et 4', homily 33 for 53); 'Remigian codex' presumably from St Remi, Reims. Line 12: 'n. ! i' read as n. 11.

nodes.text: TREATISE AGAINST FIVE HERESIES, OR AGAINST FIVE KINDS OF ENEMIES.

CHAPTER ONE. — 1. Five kinds of enemies. I am a debtor, I admit, not under the compulsion of necessity, but, what is stronger, of love. A creditor cannot be as troublesome in pressing [for payment] as a debtor is devoted to repaying. But so that I may fulfil what I promised, help me with your holy prayers, so that, with the grace of almighty God present to my words, I may also satisfy your pious minds and ears. If those of you who were present at the time are good enough to remember, we said that there are five kinds of enemies, and to defeat them we asked for a truce, so that we could prepare the necessary weapons. The promised day has dawned, and we too have come out briskly to the contest with the Lord's help. Our help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Ps. 123:8). He who gave the boldness to fight will give victory to the one who fights. Let not the crowd of enemies, nor the look of the combatants, turn us back, nor let their weapons, gleaming as if [made] of glass, terrify us. Goliath, great, strong, with terrifying weapons and protected by a huge crowd, was laid low by David alone, a small boy and unarmed, with a single blow of a stone, and he threw the whole camp of the Philistines into confusion and put [it] to flight (1 Kings 17:49). And what did the stone thrown against Goliath by David's hand signify, if not Christ, who was to come from the seed of David against the devil?

2. Let us now advance, and set out the five kinds of error we mentioned. The pagans say: Why is it that you shudder at us and reject us as worshippers of many gods? Look, you too say that the God whom you preach should be worshipped has a son, and you invent [the story] that he was born without union with the other sex. The Jews say: How do you worship one God, when you also call a man whom our fathers crucified 'Lord', and force people to venerate and worship him with you as the Son of God? The Manichees say that it is a phantasm when it is said that the Lord Christ could be born from a woman's womb. For it is not fitting, they say, that so great a majesty should be believed to have passed through the filth and squalor of a woman. The Sabellians, who are also the Patripassians, say: The Father and the Son are one God, since he who is the Father is himself also the Son. For if we say otherwise, we shall be called worshippers of many [gods]. The Arians say: The Father is one, the Son is another, but the Son is less. For how can it be that the begotten is equal to the begetter?

CHAPTER II. — 3. Confidence against the heretics. See, the questions of the errors have been set out, like the battle lines of enemies drawn up. Against these pestilent battle lines, most holy brothers, take up the armour of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day, and, perfect in all things, to stand. Gird your loins with truth: let no one tremble, let no one be afraid. There is the breastplate of righteousness, there is the shield of faith, on which the fiery arrows of the wicked may be caught and quenched. There is the helmet of salvation, there is the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6:14-17). Whoever of the faithful soldiers of Christ is protected by these arms will not fear the person of anyone, nor will he be called back from the contest by the terror of the times. Come, brothers, the contest is at hand, the work is in full heat, the adversary presses on, he gets his darts ready, he tries to throw [them]: let no one be dismayed. Brothers, there are more with us than with them. With us is Moses, that great friend of God, who, in order to defeat the enemy in battle, stretched out his hands to heaven, already then showing the figure of the cross of Christ; he, at God's command, with a single stroke of his rod, turned the waves of the swelling sea, rolling in winding curves, into dry plains for the people to cross. With us is Jesus [Joshua], leader of the people of Israel after Moses, a very brave warrior, whose very name indicates the Saviour; he, by his power and his confidence in God, halted the day so that it would not complete the course it was set, and commanded the night not to come on. He conquered, captured, humbled and killed kings of the nations, not one by one, but gathered together. With us is David, strong of hand — what shall I say? — servant of God, chosen of God, friend of God, ancestor of God: he knew, and knew well, not only how to spare the subjected and war down the proud (Aeneid 6.853), but also how to show virtues and keep patience. When he was pursuing his enemies, he was not destructive, and when he conquered, he did not prove impious. With us are other holy men, one after another, who foresaw and foretold all things to come. So there is nothing to frighten you: only wait, listen and pray. Let your prayer for me be more intent and more abundant. Let us not delay longer; let us now pursue what we have set out.

CHAPTER III. — 4. From Hermes and the Sibyl against the pagans. What do you say, pagan? God, you say, if he took delight in a son, needed a wife; if he shrank from marriage, he is alone without a son. For what could be found like God, to be joined to God and bear a son to God? Then, if, as you say, God has a son, you no longer worship one God. What are we to do? We have caught a spear thrown by the Philistine; what shall we throw back? Whatever spear we throw, even if it reaches him, it does no good. Why? Because he is hard. How hard is he? He is made of stone: he worships idols, and it is written, Let all who make them become like them, and all who trust in them (Ps. 113:8). He does not accept the holy Scriptures. So let us look for a stone with which he may be struck, so that, struck, he may be shaken; shaken, broken up; broken up, turned to dust; turned to dust, rained upon; rained upon, sown; sown, may bear fruit — not [fruit] to be consumed by fire, but to be stored in the barn. Hermes, who in Latin is called Mercury, wrote a book which is called Logos teleios, that is, The Perfect Word: a great title for this book, because great is he about whom it was written. For what is more perfect than the Word, who alone is free among the dead (Ps. 87:6)? Let us hear what Mercury says about the perfect Word: The Lord, he says, and maker of all gods, made a second Lord. And a little after, to show what he had said, he repeated it and said: Since, then, he made this one first, and alone and one, and he seemed good to him and most full of all good things. How most full? Let John the evangelist say: Of his fullness we have all received, grace for grace (John 1:16). And he seemed good to him and most full of all good things. And it continues: He rejoiced. In whom, or with whom, did he rejoice? Let the Wisdom of God itself, the Son of God, say: I was the one in whom he rejoiced (Prov. 8:30). So, he rejoiced, and loved [him] greatly as his only-begotten. The one he first called made, he afterwards called only-begotten. Again, in another place he spoke thus: The Son of the blessed God and of good will, whose name cannot be told by human mouth. Were you looking, pagan, for God's wife? Hear Mercury: get your forehead ready, and, stone, receive the stone: fall, so that you may be raised; be broken, so that you may be made firm; be pulled down, so that you may be built up. Let the blow of the stone not split the skin of the forehead, not burst a vein of blood, not open the pit of a wound, but make the sign of the cross. Are you looking for God's wife? Let impure depravity be cast out of your heart, I beg you. God's wife is good will. But how the Father is God and the Son is God, and yet they are not two gods but one God, I ought not to dispute with you, because unless you believe, you will by no means be able to understand. And yet Mercury acknowledges that the Son of God is God. Struck by this stone, let the sacrilegious man cease to be [made] of stone. Let us hear also what the Sibyl, their prophetess, says about the same: God, she says, gave another to the sons of men to be worshipped. As appears, by these sayings of Mercury and the Sibyl Sabellius too is condemned. Mercury calls both the Father and the Son God; and the Sibyl speaks of another God. Sabellius says not another, because he asserts that the Father is the same as the Son. It is very good indeed if we strike with one blow not just one, but as many adversaries as the [spear], once thrown, can reach. Again the Sibyl says: Know that your Lord himself is the Son of God. This verse rebukes both the pagan and the Jew. In another place she calls the Son of God symboulos, that is, counsel or counsellor. And the prophet says: His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God strong and mighty (Isa. 9:6). Here the Arian is refuted, who, when he says the Son of God is less, says that God at some time did not have a son. And if he was without a son, he was without counsel. See into what great dangers we are challenged. But since God was never without counsel, even though the Arian contradicts it, the Father could never be without the Son. What are you doing, pagan? Open your ears; do not be like the deaf asp, which stops its ear so as not to hear the voice of the charmer (Ps. 57:5). I am not bringing forward my own authorities to you; Mercury is yours, to whom so much honour and worship among the gods was paid by you that you named a day after him. Hear him, let him convict you, let him defeat you, so that when he has conquered you, you may yield to him and believe me. Mercury said: God loved his Only-begotten. He said: The Son of the blessed God and of good will. And so as not to bear the weariness of being questioned about his name, he went on to add: Whose name cannot be told by human mouth. What, Mercury? Do you say the name of the Son of God cannot be told by human beings? Let it be told by you, who are thought by human beings to be not a man but a god. And he speaks to his son, saying: But there is. Who? The word of wisdom of the ineffable Son, holy, holy. Is this not, In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1)? Tell [us], Hermes, does this word of wisdom have a mother? It continues: It is from God the Lord alone, God who rules over all mortals. And since it cannot be searched out by human beings, he adds and says: It is above human beings. So, since it is above human beings, I cannot tell the name of the Son of God, because I am not a god: let human beings, being human, say what I am not; I acknowledge what I am. The word of wisdom is from God alone. So do not suspect or imagine, pagan, that there was a human marriage there: it is from God alone, and it is above human beings. The Sibyl rebukes you, saying, Know that your Lord himself, the Son of God, is God: himself, not another, not Mars, not Jupiter, not Mercury, but the one whom Mercury acknowledges. Why are you surprised, Christian, that these say such things about the Father and the Son? The demons too believe, and tremble (James 2:19). Indeed in the Gospel, as the Lord passes by, they say: We know who you are, the Son of God; you have come before the time to torment us (Mark 1:24). If only human beings would acknowledge the Saviour as the demons do the judge!

CHAPTER IV. — 5. From the Old Testament against the Jews. What does the Jew say? We have one God; besides him we know no other. But the one you call Christ, our fathers killed not as God but as a man. This, indeed, is what I said: If only human beings would acknowledge the Saviour as the demons do the judge! See, the demons saw, and trembled; human beings saw, and killed. The demons confessed; human beings persecuted. What misfortune is it, and how great a misery, to be found inferior even to demons? Again, human beings believe, demons perish; human beings are saved, demons are punished. But this change is the grace of the right hand of the Most High (Ps. 76:11), not the presumption of a man trusting in his own strength. Against this Jew, however, I do not toil: his own books fight against him, the Law and the Prophets fight; and either, conquered and humbled, he will be saved, or, proud and stubborn, he will be punished. The Lord said to Moses: See, I am sending my angel to go before you and guard you on the way, and bring you into the place I have prepared. Heed him, and hear his voice, and do not think he is to be despised. You have heard 'angel'; recognise the Lord: and do not think he is to be despised. Hear further something to fear: And do not think, he says, he is to be despised. Why? Because he will not forgive you when you sin, and my name is in him (Exod. 23:20-21). Who is this one so great, to whom God gave both his power and his name? The Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory (Ps. 23:10). And how do we prove that when 'angel' is said, God ought to be understood? You have [it] in the book which is called Genesis: Two angels, it says, came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting before the gates of the city; and when he saw them, he rose and went to meet them (Gen. 19:1). What more? He received them and served them as strangers. By his habit of hospitality he was freed from the danger of the city, and both escaped the temporal fire and obtained the eternal reward. Learn, Christians, to show hospitality without discrimination, lest perhaps the one to whom you have shut your house, to whom you have refused kindness, be Christ himself. Let us not wander further from the business we set out. The angels came to Lot and said — see and note, because angels are said to speak. What did the angels say? Save your life, do not look behind you (ibid. 17). For no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). Do not stay in any of the surrounding region; do not cling to earthly pleasures, but save yourself on the mountain (Gen. 19:17); let God be your hope, lest you too perish along with the Sodomites. And Lot said to them — see a man who sees, not blind, like the Jews and the Sabellians, not bleary-eyed, like the Arians, but having healthy eyes, like the catholic Christians. He saw angels, and understood the Lord. What did he say to the angels? And Lot said to them: My Lord, since your servant has found favour before you, and you have magnified your mercy which you have shown me, in saving my life (ibid. 19). A great thing: when I want to strike the Jew in this way, Moses, a very brave man, brandished the spear of his word and threw it, so that it passed through the Jew to the Sabellian and struck the Arian. What are you doing, holy Lot? You see angels, and not one but two, and you say, My Lord. You address one, you entreat one: and are you not afraid of seeming to wrong the other? Far from it, he says. Withdraw, Jews; withdraw, Sabellians, because you do not see; withdraw, Arians, because you see too little. I see; and what I see, because I see, I neither despise nor mistake. I see two, I see [them] equal. I ask one, I wrong no one, because I do not divide the Father from the Son. And so that you may understand that I am not deceived when I entreat two as one, see whether two or one answers my prayers. He asked that he might have refuge and live in a small city nearby. It is answered to him. Let us see how many there are who answer. The words of the book follow: And he said to him — the reply is, as it were, singular. Follow further, let us see: See, I have granted your prayers in this also, that I will not overthrow the city for which you have spoken. Hurry, and be saved there, because I shall not be able to do anything until you enter there (ibid. 21-22). Do you see, Jew, that he is both called an angel and is God? Do you hear, Arian, that he speaks of two, the Father and the Son — and yet not that the Father is the same as the Son, on account of the Sabellians, but the Father and the Son? Do you hear what was said, I have granted your prayers? Do you hear what he says, I will not overthrow the city? Do you hear, I shall not be able to do anything? Let the Jew read 'angel' and understand God; let the Sabellian read that two came; let the Arian read that one answered: and let them not despise [this], but flee error, lest they come to the fire. But to show more fully that the one called an angel ought to be understood as God, let us recite what follows in this reading: Then, it says, the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven (Gen. 19:24). What is 'the Lord from the Lord', if not the Son from the Father? As also in another place: The Lord said to my Lord, that is, the Father to his Son, Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet (Ps. 109:1). Likewise in Exodus: The angel of the Lord, it says, appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the bush, and he saw that the bush was burning with fire, but the bush was not consumed. And Moses said: I will go over and see this great sight, why indeed the bush is not burnt. And when the Lord saw that he was coming near to see, the Lord called him from the bush. See, the angel himself is the Lord himself. And it continues, saying: Moses, Moses. And he said: Who are you, Lord? The Lord said to him: Do not come near here unless you have taken the sandals off your feet; for the place on which you stand is holy ground. Hear further what he said to him: I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob (Exod. 3:2-6). And so let the Jew hear 'angel' in such a way as to understand the Lord and fear God; let the Sabellian confess the Father in such a way as not to deny the Son; let the Arian confess the Father and the Son in such a way as not to diminish the Son. Jesus [Joshua] the son of Nun also, as the book written under his name says, when he was fighting against the enemy, standing in battle array itself, saw a man standing facing him and holding a drawn sword; and he went up to him and said: Are you ours, or our adversaries'? He answered: Not at all, but I am the commander of the army of the Lord, and now I have come (Josh. 5:13-14). And Jesus fell face down on the ground and worshipped. And now, Jew, follow your leader. He sees, he asks, and he worships. Seeing is shared: for both what is recognised and what is not recognised is seen. So seeing is shared, asking [marks] ignorance, worship [marks] faith. Whom does he see? A man. Who is this man? He is the one whose coming against the hostile nations was foretold, longed for, awaited. [And he is a man, it says, and who will know him?] Who is the commander of the army of the Lord? Is it not he who, when asked in the Gospel who he was, answered: The Beginning, who also speak to you (John 8:25)? Why are you troubled, Jesus? Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. 2:1)? You see an armed man; do not be afraid: I do not come against you, but for you, because I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24). What is it, Jesus, that you see, ask and worship? Listen: I see a man; I ask whom I see; I hear whom I do not see; I worship not what I see but what I believe, because faith [comes] from hearing, and hearing through the word of God (Rom. 10:17). What then do you ask? Pay attention, and follow: I see a man, but what I understand is beyond the sons of men. Something or other flashes before me, and something bright shines out as if from hiding. I go to him, because he has come to me: I will search out what I see, this so great vision. The one I see both is a man and is not a man. Indeed, he is a man because of the Manichee, and he is more than a man because of the Jew. Go on, my Jesus, my leader, go on. Why, unless because when you seek me, you gain me? See, I come, I find a man: within, I understand something or other; it is obscure, I do not yet see: the face of Moses is upright, [but] the veil hinders the sight (Exod. 34:33); the truth lies hidden. I do not recognise what it is; there is need of a question. Tell [me], you man, are you ours or our adversaries'? If he is of the adversaries, he is both a man and an enemy; if he is ours, he is both a man and the Saviour. After me comes [one] who was made before me (John 1:30). If he is Jesus, he is also the Saviour. Let Jesus ask Jesus, let the earlier ask the later, but nonetheless the lesser the greater; let the one who wanes ask the one who grows; let the figure ask the truth, or rather let the figure understand the truth, so that the day may dawn and the darkness of time be removed. See, I come; I know that a spirit does not have flesh and bones (Luke 24:39); I touch flesh: I seek, I gaze on an armed man. Still the mystery lies hidden. I question a man, I hear the Word; I remove the veil, I worship God. In that Jesus saw and did not recognise, he signified the raging nation of the Jews, which, if it had recognised when it saw, would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2:8); but in that by hearing he believed and worshipped, he signified this people, of whom it is written, A people whom I did not know has served me; at the hearing of the ear it has obeyed me (Ps. 17:45). Listen further, you who deny that God begot a Son; listen to what the Father says through the prophet Isaiah: Shall I, who make others give birth, not give birth myself, says the Lord (Isa. 66:9)? Shall I, who grant generation to the rest, remain barren? says the Lord your God, to whom it was said, You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7). Why do you goad me, Arian, and mock when you hear 'today'? With God there is never a tomorrow, never a yesterday, but always today: there the year does not revolve in the cycle of months, the month is not passed through by days following and departing, the hours do not change, the times or moments do not vary, where the day is neither closed by an end nor begun by a beginning. Let the Jew hear further what the Lord says through the prophet, let the Arian hear; let all those also hear who say that the Son of God either does not exist or is lesser. I, he says, am God, and there is no other. And what of the Son, Lord, if you alone are God? Listen further; why do you hurry? By myself I have sworn. Where there is an oath, there is no doubt. By myself I have sworn, The word of justice shall go forth from my mouth. See, you have the Son: The word of justice shall go forth from my mouth, and shall not return. What does 'shall not return' mean? Lest the Sabellian say that the Son is the very same as the Father, the Word that has gone forth shall not return: because the Father is the Father, the Son is the Son. Let the talkativeness of the heretics, which has no shame, be silent a little; let the Lord complete the sentence; and either no one will oppose the Son of God, or whoever has proved an adversary will be put to shame. The word of justice, he says, shall go forth from my mouth, and shall not return; because to me every knee shall bow, and every tongue shall confess. And what of the Son? Listen, then, to what is said in the Lord: Mine are the highest justice and dominion. Come then, and what after that? To him they shall come, and all who resist him shall be put to shame (Isa. 45:22-25). Go now, all of you, pagans, heretics, Jews; oppose and resist the Son of God: to him you will come, and all of you who resist him will be put to shame.

CHAPTER 5. — 6. Against the Manichees. We have spoken not a little about the Son of God according to his divinity, and as far as we could we have not spared the adversaries who resist; now I wish to come to his incarnation, and the impure Manichee stands in the way. Why? Because he does not want the Son of God to be called also the son of man. And where then is what is written, Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the just one; let the earth be opened and bud forth the Saviour; and let justice spring up together; I the Lord have created him (ibid. 45:8)? Again, See, a little child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and the government is upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of peace (Isa. 9:6)? Again, See, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23)? Someone says: You had arranged to contend with the Manichee, not with the Jew. Against the Manichee new weapons are needed, not old ones. Why? Because he accepts the New Testament, not the Old. But I, who have taken up the contest against both, need weapons from every side; above all, since these new ones were forged from the old: so those are not to be thrown away, and these are to be carried. For different adversaries fall by different weapons. So this order must be kept, that in speaking of the Gospel I am not silent about the Prophets.

7. But I, says the Manichee, accept neither Moses nor the Prophets. What do you say about the apostle Paul, who at the beginning of his Letter to the Romans wrote: Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, called an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his Prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:1-3)? Do you hear that the Gospel would not have been presented through the Apostles unless it had been promised beforehand through the Prophets? Do you hear that the Son of God according to divinity was made son of man from the seed of David according to the flesh? For in what are the Prophets contrary to the Gospel? The Prophet said: Drop down dew, you heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the just one: let the angel come, let him preach the word. Let the earth be opened: let Mary hear; and bud forth the Saviour: let her bear Jesus. The Prophet said, See, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel. The evangelist too, when he said this, followed it and explained it, saying, God with us (Matt. 1:23). In vain, Manichee, do you try to oppose the Prophets. See, the Apostle says, Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3). What the Prophets foresaw and foretold, this the Apostles saw and preached. He who was, was made. What was he? What was he made? He was the Word, he was made flesh. He was God, he was made man: he was the Son of God, he was made the Son of man. He took up humanity, he did not lose divinity: made lowly, he remained exalted; he was born a man, he did not cease to be God; he was born a little child, hidden [as] great. Let whoever gladly embraces God born not shudder at the virgin's childbirth. God, the creator of man, the son of man, says to you: What is it that disturbs you in my birth? I was not conceived by the desire of lust. I made the mother from whom I would be born; I prepared and cleansed the way for my journey. She whom you despise, Manichee, is my mother; but she was fashioned by my hand. If I could have been defiled when I made her, I could have been defiled when I was born from her. Just as her virginity was not corrupted by my passing through, so my majesty was not stained there. If a ray of the sun can dry up the filth of sewers and cannot be defiled by them, how much more can the splendour of eternal light, which no defilement touches, cleanse wherever it shines, and itself not be polluted? Fool, where is filth in the virgin mother, where there is no intercourse with a human father? Where is filth in her who suffered neither lust in conceiving nor pain in giving birth? Where is filth in a house which no inhabitant approached? Only its builder and lord came to it; he put on the garment he did not have; and as he found it, he left it closed. Just as he was born alone free among the dead (Ps. 87:6), so the chastity of this mother from whom he was born alone is intact. Eve, disobedient, earned punishment; Mary, by obeying, obtained grace: the one by tasting the forbidden [fruit] was cursed, the other by believing the angel was blessed; the one brought death to us, the other bore life for us. What are you doing, Manichee? You oppress the Christian, you do not defend Christ. Let unclean vanity be silent, because clean truth has been born.

CHAPTER VI. — 8. Against the Arians. I would like to pursue the Manichee further, but I am suffering from a hostile Arian, who trusts in his own strength and boasts in his own power (Ps. 48:7). Indeed, while we were answering the others, we were not silent about him either; but now too, keeping his own order, let us see what darts he throws. Let no one's personal power frighten [you]: All flesh is grass (Isa. 40:6). You see grass grow every day, you see it flower; why are you terrified? Such are the fruits a deserted land puts forth. I do not accuse the farmers, but I look for them. Where are you now, good farmers? What are you doing? Why are you idle? You see how many evils this land is full of: here thorns, here thistles, here grass springs up. Burn the thorns, root out the thistles, cut the grass, scatter good seed; do not let winter frighten you: and if iniquity abounds, yet let your charity burn. Sow in winter what you may reap in summer. But to whom am I speaking? Where are you, fountains of tears? To what farmers am I talking? Some are dead, others put to flight: the earth has been given into the hands of the wicked (Job 9:24); tribulation and distress have found us. Lord, give us help out of tribulation, so that the salvation of man may not be vain, but true (Ps. 59:13). What do you say, Arian? Please answer me as I question you. I do not want you to despise the little one; your great stature does not help you, your great weapons do not protect you; the blow of a single stone pierces a helmeted forehead (1 Kgs 17:49). Tell me, then, what I ask you: Do you believe in God the Father almighty? I believe, he says. Do you believe in Jesus Christ his Son our Lord? I believe, he says. Do you believe that Jesus Christ, God and man, was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary? I believe, he says. You do well. I ask further: Just as the Father is God, so is the Son also God? Yes. The Father is one, the Son another? Very much so. Is the Son equal to the Father? Equal, equal, he says. What remains? See, he has answered everything I asked. In saying that he believes in God the Father and God the Son, he is with me against the pagan. In believing that Christ, God and man, was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, he is with me against the Jew and the Manichee. In believing that the Father is one and the Son another, he is with me against the Sabellian. Come, if you are with me in everything, why are we quarrelling? If we have one inheritance, let us possess it together; we are brothers: See how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity (Ps. 132:1)! Why is there a new building in front of the wall? Let us keep watch together to guard our inheritance. Our inheritance is splendid to us (Ps. 15:6). We have envious people, we have enemies: and they too want to possess it, not with us, but against us. Let no one seize anything for himself: this inheritance was left to us in such a way that it is to be possessed undivided, not scattered in portions. Let us gather the fruit together, lest by dividing we lose it. Poverty makes me anxious; I beg you, do not gather outside, apart from me, lest you begin to scatter. For whoever does not gather with me scatters (Luke 11:23). It is as if I had forgotten with whom I was dealing; but I have not forgotten: I am questioning an Arian, whom I long to be a catholic. Someone says: He has answered everything you wanted; nothing contrary is found in his answers; what more do you seek? Wait, brother, do not judge hastily; I still have something to ask: do not quickly entrust yourself to him; the answer is clear, the poison is hidden. What did you say, brother? The Son is equal to the Father? Equal, you say. Come now, keep watch; now what was hidden will be revealed. How do you say the Son is equal to the Father? In operation, or in origin? In power, or in eternity? Or perhaps in both? Far from it, you say. He is equal in operation and power, not in eternity: for how can it be that the begotten is equal to the unbegotten? There he is, the one who was walking with me as a co-heir; the deceit that was hidden has appeared. He was thought to possess with me; he wants to divide: but I do not allow it; I resist utterly. The laws require that the will of the testator be obeyed in everything: if anyone wishes to act against the will of the testator, let him lose the inheritance. But are the laws silent among arms (Cicero, For Milo, 40)? Not at all: the labour, the fighting, is for this, that the laws may be served. I bring out the testament, I read the words of the testator: if there is anything to be divided, I find it there; if there is nothing to be divided, I answer you from the testament itself. Hear what the testament contains: My peace I give to you, peace I leave to you (John 14:27). This is the inheritance. And who is the testator himself? Read the Testament, and you will find out. When the prophet was speaking of the Lord, he said: He shall be magnified to the ends of the earth, and he shall be peace (Mic. 5:4-5). Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men (Luke 2:14); not to the dividers of holy unity, but to men of good will. He himself is the inheritance, he himself is the testator, and it is he whom you seek to divide. Why do you split what is one? If you divide what is one, you will have nothing whole. O Arian heresy, cruel and impious harlot, blush at the judgement of Solomon. A harlot, so as not to destroy one living [child], conceived from wherever, and already born, did not allow her son to be divided; and you divide the Lord your God? She, though a harlot, was yet devoted, because she was a mother; you are both a harlot and impious, because you are not a mother: what you bear you smother, what you do not bear you gather. How do you nurse another's [child], you who kill your own? Your bowels have hardened; hers trembled. What did she say? Give her the child, and do not divide him (1 Kgs 3:27). He is my son; but I would rather rejoice that he is whole and alive with her than mourn him divided and dead. He is my son, she says; but what good shall I, a mother, do the child if I take away the life I do not give? I want to keep that cruel woman's breasts from the little one, but I am forced rather to fear the judge's sword. Give her my son: he was born mine; but let him pass wholly to her, let affection remain with me. Give her the whole child, let not the life of his limbs be taken away: let his wholeness not be divided, [and] my devotion is not snatched from me. What did she say? Give her the child and do not divide him. See, I too say: possess it all, and do not divide God. No, he says; but if you want to have peace without prejudice, divide the inheritance. And how am I to divide? The Father is greater, the Son less? O portions! O justice! O equality! One portion is greater, the other less. I do not consent, I do not make a portion; because I do not divide peace. For if peace is broken, it will no longer be peace. But how can peace be unimpaired with you, in whom faith is not whole? Hence, because you will not possess with me, and want to divide peace, you cannot obtain the inheritance. Finally, if with your mouth you strive not for peace but for faithlessness, go, appeal to the judge; let us see what he will say to you. You have an ordinary judge; I do not want you to bring me other and other powers from different quarters. I need not an armour-bearer, but a lawgiver. And where, you say, am I to find him? But where will you not find him? Hear the prophet saying: The Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver. And do not think the judge is to be despised; hear what follows: The Lord is our king, the Lord himself will save us (Isa. 33:22). See, you have a judge. If that is too little, our king too is before you. He is in heaven in such a way that he does not leave the earth. I fill heaven and earth, he says (Jer. 23:24). I am with you all days, to the end of the age (Matt. 28:20). He is both with us and with the Father: for he did not leave the Father when he came down to us, nor did he forsake us when he ascended to the Father. Appeal to him, say to him: Lord, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me. Hear the divine answer, hear the just judge; hear peace fleeing from strife: what does he say? Friend, who appointed me judge or divider between you (Luke 12:13-14)? You want to divide peace, and you seek to have peace as judge? I do not want to be your judge; let me be peace; I do not know how to quarrel; I sit with those who agree, I flee those who quarrel. If, when you were an enemy of my Father, I reconciled you through myself, how then will you separate me from my Father? When you were far off, I came to bring you back; when you were wandering among mountains and forests, I sought you; among stones and wood I found you: you stumbled on stones, you clung to them, because you worshipped wood and stones. And lest you be torn by the greedy jaws of wolves and wild beasts, I gathered you, I carried you on my shoulders, I gave you back to my Father; I laboured, I sweated, I put my head under thorns, I offered my hands to nails, a lance opened my side: I was torn by so many — I will not say injuries, but harsh sufferings: I shed my blood, I laid down my life, to join you to myself; and you divide me? Hear what answer is given to the disciple who knew the Son and was seeking the Father. Philip says to the Lord: Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us. Was not he too separating the Son from the Father? We know you already, he says, but we do not know your Father. And what do you want? Show us the Father, and it is enough for us. And the Lord [said] to him — if you are willing to hear, Arian: you erred with the apostle, come back with the apostle; let his rebuke be your cure too. What does the Lord say? Have I been with you so long, he says, and you have not known me? Philip, I came to join you to my Father; do not separate me: why do you seek as it were another besides me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also. So great is the unity in us, so great the likeness, so great the charity, that I am in the Father, and the Father in me. I sense, Sabellian, what you are muttering: you hasten either to shut me in with the Arian or to call me away from the Arian. But in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit — not of three gods, but of one God — while I answer him, I do not pass you by. What did the Lord say? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also. Did he say, Whoever has seen me has seen the Father; or, I am at once Son and Father? But he said, I am in the Father, and the Father in me; and, Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also (John 14:8-10). The insertion of one syllable, the one called 'also', distinguishes the Father and distinguishes the Son; and shows that you have neither the Father nor the Son. Tell me, Arian: do you call the Father God? Very much so. What of the Son? I confess him too to be God. How do you recognise [this]? Because when he was foretold as coming in the flesh, the prophet said of him: Say, you faint-hearted, be strengthened: do not fear; see, our God will bring the vengeance of recompense; God himself will come and save us (Isa. 35:4). Acknowledge [it], in what you say you acknowledge, if you do not oppose the Prophet. What then do you say of the Father? He is God. What of the Son? He is God. Is the Son co-eternal with the Father? No. Then, according to you, there was a time when the Son was not. If there was a time when the Son was not, then there was a time which the Son did not make. If there was a time which the Son did not make, not all things were made through him: for there was already a time when the Son was not. If there was a time when the Son was not, John the evangelist ought not to have said, In the beginning was the Word, but, In the beginning was time. John says, All things were made through him (John 1:1, 3); but the Arian contradicts. Tell me, Arian: how do you know that there was a time when the Son was not? Or perhaps you will say: And how does John know that in the beginning was the Word? Because he reclined on the Lord's breast, and from there he drew what he drank at Christ's banquet: that in the beginning was the Word. Yet tell me: when in the beginning was the Word (ibid. 1), or when John was reclining on the Lord's breast (John 13:23) and learning from the Word of the Lord that the Word was in the beginning and the Word was God, where was Arius? I do not know whether you dare say he was there. For it is known, and it is read, at what time he was born, and how deservedly he was condemned. It is known too how he lived and how he died: and therefore you do not dare say of Arius, as of the Word, He both was and is; because Arius neither was then, nor is now. But so that the Arian may be shut out on every point, hear what is said through Solomon: The Lord made the regions and the uninhabitable bounds under heaven. When he was preparing the heaven, I was present with him. And a little after: I was with him, ordering all things; I was [there] when he made the strong foundations of the earth; I was the one in whom he rejoiced (Prov. 8:26-27, 30). But you say: The question is about time, whether the Son existed before there was time. Hear him saying through the prophet: From time, he says. What does 'from time' mean? Was it from when time began to be? Not so, impious Arian, not so: but, From time, before it was made, I was there (Isa. 48:16). See, before time was made, he was there. Now look for when he was not, who was before times. In the beginning was the Word. The Greeks say it better, Logos; for it signifies both word and reason. So you see that he always was, of whom you dare to say, He was not. Or if you say that God was at some time without word or without reason, you will now be an adversary not only to the Son but also to the Father. I, he says, came forth from the mouth of the Most High (Ecclus. 24:5). Who says this? The Word. And what is this Word? Let John say: The Word was God. So both the Word, and he whose Word it was, are not two but one. No, you say: because a word is later than the one whose word it is; whence it appears that the Son is less than the Father. So you deny that the Son of God is God. I do not deny it, you say: I call the Father God and the Son God; but the Father greater, the Son less. How long is the Father greater, the Son less? Tell me, since I see you want to trample on eternity: by how many years does God the Father precede his Son? Where did you read of the birthday of the Son of God? I say of the Son of God; I do not say of the Son of God and man. Where then did you read of his birthday? With what astrologer did you seek out and work through the horoscope of the Creator of the stars? What times, what hours, what moments, what numbers, what minutes of the moments of the birth of him who founded all things have you gathered? Let it rest, I beg, let it rest, this heretical thing of yours, not religion but superstition: calculation fails concerning the beginning of Christ. For when eternity without beginning is heard of, no age is sought for it. If the Father is God and the Son is God, the Father greater, the Son less, then there is no longer one God, but two gods. If there are two gods, what then is it that the Lord says through the prophet, Before me no God was formed, and after me there will be none (Isa. 43:10)? What do you say, Arian? To whom do you assign these words? If they are the Father's, then by saying, Before me no God was formed, and after me there will be none, either he himself will not be Father, or the Son will not be God. For if he said only this, Before me no God was formed, and did not add, and after me there will be none, you would be free to apply these words to the Father alone. But since he goes on and says, after me there will be none, then according to you, as I said, he denies both that he himself is Father and that the Son is God. Again, if these words are the Son's, he denies his Father to be both God and Father. For if he did not say, Before me no God was formed, but said only, after me there will be none, it might perhaps be said that the Son had spoken it. But now, when he says, Before me no God was formed, and after me there will be none, he says that his Father is neither God nor Father. Again, if these words are the Father's, who says, and to whom does he say, You are my Son, today I have begotten you (Ps. 2:7)? Or is God perhaps, which God forbid, to be convicted of a lie? But if they are the Son's words, who says, and of whom does he say, My Father is working until now (John 5:17)? Or is he perhaps to be judged both insulting to the Father and ungrateful? But would it be said to an ungrateful one, Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession (Ps. 2:8)? Or did the Prophet perhaps not know what he was saying, or want to deceive; or, to say something milder of the Prophet, is he to be believed to have imagined two people talking together, that is, the Father and the Son, and when the Father said, Before me no God was formed, the Son joined in saying, And after me there will be none? Is what we are dealing with mime and farce, or divine things? O crime! O grief! Spare us, spare us, heretical impiety. Since you cannot grasp God, you provoke us too to blasphemy. The holy Church does not teach this. The Father is Father; the Son is Son: and the one was never not Father, and the other was never not Son: both eternal, they neither began to be nor cease. What the Father speaks, the Son speaks, because he is the Word of the Father; and what the Son speaks, the Father speaks, because he is the Father of the Word. The Word himself says, The words that I speak, I do not speak of myself (John 14:10). Grant, I beg you, to the Creator what he himself has granted to the creature, and in the created thing, if you can, grasp the Creator. See, fire and brightness are two; one is from the other, and neither is without the other: the fire is the father, the brightness the son. The brightness, if it could, would say, That I shine, I do not shine of myself; but he who sent me, he gave me to shine. For fire sends out brightness. And just as the Son says of God the Father, The Father is with me (John 16:32), so the brightness too could say, The fire is with me. Put out the fire, and the brightness will appear nowhere. If then fire and brightness, father and son, the one a father without a wife, the other a son without a mother, cannot be divided one from the other; and though one is from the other, yet the beginning of the one cannot be without the other; and if this power has been granted by the Creator to the creature: what can the Creator himself do? Let the pagan come near, let the Sabellian come near, let the Arian come near: let them contemplate a lamp, and see in it what they cannot see in God. I do no wrong if, wishing to show in some part the power of so great a Creator, I bring forward so slight a likeness as fire or a lamp. For it is written, Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths (Ps. 118:105). And of God it is said, A consuming fire (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29). Come near, then, and consider the lamp carefully, and put away your foolish darkness. Let the pagan look, and learn there that Father and Son are without marriage, and how the Son was born: and if you are not blind, see there; look for something in between the fire and the brightness. If there is nothing in between, there is no marriage. Do not try to search out something in between, lest you suffer a great burning. Let the Sabellian come near, let him see two in one, fire and brightness. Could not the brightness rightly say, I am in the fire, and the fire in me, just as the Son says, I am in the Father, and the Father in me (John 14:10)? Let the Arian also come near; let him too see one from the other, and yet that the one cannot be born without the other: neither of them is earlier, neither later; father and son, brightness and fire, are of the same age: neither can fire be without brightness, nor brightness without fire. Or certainly, if you like, put out your hand, divide the one from the other: show me fire without brightness, or brightness without fire. Far from it, far from it: you will only be able to burn yourself; you will not be able to separate the one from the other. For just as fire and brightness are one from the other, and yet the one cannot be without the other, so God the Father and God the Son are one from the other, and yet the one cannot be without the other. They have no rising, which is not, but an eternity and one substance. Fire and brightness are temporal; but the Father and the Son, God, are eternal. I say 'are', because [they are] Father and Son; I say 'God', because they are one. Duality in the offspring, unity in the deity. The birth of the one makes another, but the divinity shows them to be one. When I say 'Son', he is another; when I say 'God', he is one. He is another [person], because he is Son; he is not another thing, because he is God. Blush, Arians. Pilate's executioners did not dare to tear the tunic of a man already condemned and hanging on the cross (John 19:24): and do you try to divide the love of God who sits in heaven, or rather God who is love itself? But try; try as hard as you can; you have already fallen headlong into hell: for that tunic you will never rend. Again, through the prophet the Lord says, There is no God apart from me: a just and saving God there is none besides me (Isa. 45:21).

CHAPTER 7. — 9. Against Sabellius. Here the Sabellian exults. For in order to show that the Father and the Son are one and the same, he believes himself fortified by such testimonies. The Arians on the other side, to prove that the Father is one and the Son another, bring forward other testimonies, and say: The Father is so far one and the Son another, and the one greater, the other less, that the Father says to the Son, I have given you as a light to the nations (Isa. 49:6), and the Son says, The Father sent me (John 8:19). As far as I understand, this light of the nations is so clear and transparent that the heretics, not able to grasp it or see it clearly, and so blinded by it, cannot walk in it, but rather wander astray. The Arian says one thing, the Sabellian another. What a war! What does the Catholic say to this? The arms, he says, which they carry are mine: they fight for me; both fight against each other, but on my behalf: would that both would give out, and that neither would go over to the other, but to me! Let me too bring something forward, by which both may be struck. You, Arian, say that he who sends is greater, he who is sent is less: I too ask you, Who is greater, he who goes before, or he before whom one goes? Again, who is greater, he for whom something is prepared when he comes, or he who prepares it; he to whom a service is rendered, or he who renders it? Surely, if you ask the human race, it will answer that he is greater before whom one goes, for whom things are prepared, or to whom service is rendered. You want to prove from this that the Son is less, because he was sent: I show that he who sent goes before him whom he sent; and I do not call either of them greater, because I do not dare to call [either] less. The prophet Isaiah says, Thus says the Lord to my Christ the Lord, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before his face. See, the Father is now the companion of the Son who was sent. Follow further: And I will turn the backs of kings, and I will open doors before him, and the gates will not be shut (Isa. 45:1). See, he who had sent has become the forerunner. For what greater or superior person opens doors before a lesser? Or how would he do it, unless he also went a little ahead? Hear further: And the gates, he says, will not be shut. How? I will go before you (ibid., 2). You see that he who had sent both accompanies and goes before: he sends, and does not depart. It is not enough that he does not depart; he also goes before. Now distinguish who is greater, who superior: for I see no distinction, but rather behold equality. The Son says of the Father, He sent me (John 8:46). The Father says to the Son, I will go before you. Let quarrelsome calamity withdraw from our midst: equality shows this, not disparity. Follow further, so that it may appear more clearly who says this to whom: I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious of the earth. Be here too, pagan. Hear what the prophet says. I have not written what I wished for myself: the book in which these things are read written is kept in the Jew's book-chest. My enemy is my witness; ask him; open, read, and believe. I will turn, he says, the backs of kings, and humble the glorious of the earth. Do you not see that the kings of the earth, who formerly persecuted Christians, are now Christians? Do you not see those who humbled the Church entering the Church humbly? Do you not see that it now has as defenders the very ones it formerly had as persecutors? I, he says, will go before you, and humble the glorious of the earth. I will break the gates of bronze and shatter the bars of iron. And I will give you hidden treasures and the mysteries of secret things, that you may know that I am God, who call your name, the God of Israel (Isa. 45:2–3). Let the Sabellian hear: God speaks, he speaks to God. So there are two: he who speaks and he to whom he speaks. Let the Arian also hear: I am God, and there is no other besides me (ibid., 5). It is a long time now that I have laboured, contending against these two heresies, and I am almost worn out. Come, my Lord Jesus, mightiest warrior, prince of the army of the Lord, who conquered the devil and the world: Take hold of arms and shield, and rise up to help me (Ps. 34:2). When he was about to go forth to battle and to conquer the world in the world, he prayed; not as lacking power, since he was almighty, but to show us the teaching of humility, for which he had come. And what did he say? Father, glorify your Son (John 17:1). Now the accursed Arian says, Do you see that he is less, and would not have glory unless he had asked the Father? Wait, man, why do you hurry? You see the man, in which form he is less not only than the Father but also than the angels (Ps. 8:6): the man appears, God lies hidden. You show me a humble man: open your eyes and see God on high, not less than the angels, but equal to the Father. Father, he says, glorify your Son: see, less. Follow further: That your Son also may glorify you (John 17:1): see, equal. We have found the Son acknowledging the Father, and praying, and joined to him, not ungrateful as was supposed. Let us see what the Father too says of the Son. Jesus took Peter and James and John his brother (these are the Gospel's words), and led them up a high mountain apart, and was transfigured before them. And his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as snow. And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, talking with him (Matt. 17:1–3). Moses and Elijah, the Law and the Prophets; they were talking with him, because they had spoken of him; they were showing him whom they had foretold, making manifest him whom they had prophesied. They were talking: what, do you think, were they talking of? That the Jews might be convicted, the pagans converted, the Manichees confounded, the heretics suppressed, the Catholics strengthened. There talked together light and grace, harshness and gentleness, terror and mildness, precept and help, the knife and the physician, shadow and light, herald and judge, sentence and mercy. And what after this? Peter answered and said to Jesus: Lord, it is good for us to be here; if you wish, let us make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah (Matt. 17:4). What are you saying, holy Peter? The world is in labour, and you seek seclusion? You see so many nations come together into one, and you seek rest? You see the darkness of the world, and you hide the light? No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house (Matt. 5:15). This house is the whole world: the lighting of the lamp is the incarnation of the Word; the lampstand is the wood of the cross; the lamp shining on the lampstand is Christ hanging on the cross. No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. You have seen; let us see too. It is dark; let us not stumble among the pagans, let us not stray among the heretics: let the lamp shine for us, let the Word in the flesh teach us. Let us see what the Evangelist says, let us see whether Peter's counsel was accepted: While he was still speaking, he says, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. And behold, a voice from the cloud saying (Matt. 17:5). Let us all listen, let no one shut his ears. Let the mocking pagans hear, let the persecuting Jews hear, let the Manichees, dreamers of phantasms, hear, let the heretics, erring litigants, hear; let them hear, and let the Catholics too hear most of all, the faithful worshippers of God. Let these hear so that they may be instructed, those so that they may be corrected: or let these hear so that they are not led astray, those so that they may be punished. What does the voice from the cloud say? This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (ibid., and 3:17). Where are you who oppose the Son of God? The Father says, This is my Son: and you say, God has no Son. You, pagan, why do you stand outside and grumble? Come in here into God's school, open the ears of your heart, hear the voice of the Lord, and learn the Son of God. What will you do, Jews, who killed the Son of God? Where will you flee, where will you hide yourselves? What mountains, what rocks are going to fall upon you? And if you hide yourselves in the caves of the rocks, from there I will drag you out, says the Lord (Jer. 49:16). But you too, come, enter, hear my counsel, do not despair: for there is a remnant for the peaceable man (Ps. 36:37). You raged, you killed, you shed the blood of Christ; you are in danger, you were unbelieving towards the Son of God. What then do you have to do now, except to believe and be baptised, and drink the blood that you shed? There is nothing for you to shudder at: the physician's blood was shed, and it became the medicine of the madman. Why do you hesitate? Taste, and see that the Lord is sweet (Ps. 33:9). What, you Manichee, how long will you dream of phantasms? Wake up, and see; the clouds thunder. What do they thunder? This is my beloved Son (Matt. 3:17; 17:5). See on earth a true man, hear from heaven the true God: see on earth the son of man, hear from heaven that he is the Son of God. Recognise that both are true, that is, God and man: that the Son of God and the son of man are one and the same, God and man. Acknowledge the man, and you will appease God. Beware lest you stumble on the rock and suffer the ruin of death: for what you dream is vanity; what God thunders is truth. Hear, you Sabellian, hear the Father from heaven, see the Son on earth, and do not say, The Father is the same as the Son. Hear, you Arian too, and do not go astray concerning the Father and the Son, but follow the unity, and see the divinity. Lord, let us hear what you say of your Son: This is, he says, my Son. See on earth the son of man, hear from heaven that he is the Son of God. My beloved, in whom I am well pleased. And what [else]? Listen to him. Thanks be to God. The command of God has thundered, and Peter's counsel has been set aside. Thanks to you, God the Power; thanks to you, God the Father, who have both shown your Son and given me a teacher. Let the Sabellian withdraw, let the Arian withdraw, let the other plagues withdraw, let every wicked doctrine withdraw. Let God teach, not Arius: let the Son of God teach, not the Son's adversary. Speak, my Lord Jesus, teach, [that] I may learn what I am to teach. The Sabellian says, The Father is the very same as the Son. The Arian says, The Father is one, the Son another; the Father greater, the Son lesser. He opposes, shouts, quarrels, fights, gathers mobs, battles against Christ. He [Christ] shed blood, to redeem; this man scatters money, to destroy. He builds a cave, there he chokes the Catholic, he calls the Christian a pagan, he forces Baptism on the baptised, contrary to what is written, He who has once been washed does not need to be washed again (John 13:10). The man cries out, I am a Christian: why do you say I am what I am not? He cries out, I am one of the faithful: and that man says, Take money from me. He cries out, I have been redeemed: and that man says, Take gold from me. What do you give, or what do you take away? You give money, to take away grace: you give money, to take away life: you give a price, to take away that for which I was bought. What do you buy from one already bought? My price is not gold, but the blood of Christ: you do not lead me astray, you do not deceive me; however much you bestow on me, you do not take my price from me. Your money go with you to perdition (Acts 8:20): for my price has no price. The man cries out: I am one of the faithful, and you breathe out [on me in exorcism]. He cries out, I was baptised in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and you breathe out. What then do you leave for the Christian, in whom you breathe out against the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit? Or have you perhaps brought a new faith, a new baptism, a new god from overseas? Speak, my teacher, holy Paul, teach, you expert in divine law, friend of the bridegroom: this man has just come, he overturns the world, and tears the unity of the faith. He divides the Trinity, he strives to rebaptise one who does not agree with him; what am I to do? In Christ Jesus himself, through the Gospel, you begot me (1 Cor. 4:15); in Christ I was baptised. Is there perhaps another baptism or another faith? Far from it, you say: One faith, one Baptism, one God and Father of all (Eph. 4:5–6). If then there is one faith, or rather because there is indeed one faith, one Baptism, one God and Father of all: I have already believed, I have already been baptised, I already have God as Father: why do I suffer the Arian murderer? Help, my Lord Jesus, and gird your sword upon your thigh, most mighty (Ps. 44:4). Mightiest of all, go forth, slay them in themselves, so that they may live in you, and cease to persecute me. The Sabellians take you away, the Arians diminish you: what do you say of yourself? The Father said that we should listen to you: when we listen to you, we listen to him: strike both adversaries with one blow. Let them perish, he says, the vain talkers and deceivers of the mind, the Arian and the Sabellian: for I and the Father are one (John 10:30). He did not say, I and the Father am one; but, I and the Father are one. When I say 'one', let the Arian hear: when I say 'are', let the Sabellian hear. Let the Arian not divide the 'one': let the Sabellian not delete the 'are': but let both come, and let them too be one in us, just as I and the Father are one (John 17:11). Therefore if the Father and the Son are one, or rather because without doubt they are one, not two gods but one God: the prophet wrote nothing theatrical, but spoke the truth, when the Lord said, Before me no God was formed, and after me there will be none (Isa. 43:10). Truth has taught the truth, and with a two-edged sword has slain every error. If the heretics still resist, let the Catholics hear the definitive judgement, which they are to follow.

CHAPTER VIII. — 10. Conclusion. You have heard what the Father said of the Son, you have heard what the Son said of the Father or of himself. If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you have received, let him be anathema (Gal. 1:8). We have said of the Father and the Son what we could, and as much as we could, if indeed we could say anything worthily. Of the Holy Spirit we have been silent; but we have not separated him; for whatever we have said of the Father and the Son, we have said also of the Holy Spirit. For he is in them and with them, equal and one, not a lesser or a third god. What else shall I, weary, say to you who are weary? Whoever separates the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in eternity and substance or communion, and whoever denies that the Holy Spirit is of the Father and the Son, is full of an unclean spirit, empty of the Holy Spirit. For God is called love (1 John 4:8) for this reason, that he does not divide the unity into parts, but ineffably binds together the Trinity. For the Trinity itself is one God, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy (Ps. 60:4), who guards those who believe in him for ever and ever. Amen.

This sermon too was delivered under the domination of the Arians, at a time when no one dared to resist those heretics as they disputed and strove to draw the Catholics away from the faith, some by promises and rewards, others by force and power. You think yourself great, says the preacher in ch. 1, because you dispute with no one arguing against you, with no judge presiding. And while the times favour your error, you think yourself something, though you are nothing: and, led astray, you desire to lead many astray, some by money, some by power. Compare this with the preceding sermon, ch. 7, in which place, namely above, col. 1115, line 11, you will observe that the Church of the Arians is called a cave, as here in ch. 11. In chs. 3 and 4 the baptised are admonished to fulfil the profession of their renunciation, just as in the spurious sermons on the Creed to the Catechumens in vol. 6. Other passages similar to those, or to the preceding sermon, we pass over. Many things, moreover, are drawn from Augustine: the passage in ch. 18, Surely if he brought it about by magic arts that he was worshipped when dead, he was not a magician before he was born? is from book 1 of On the Agreement of the Evangelists, ch. 11. Likewise the passage in ch. 13, What is In the midst of two living creatures you will be known, except either in the midst of the two Testaments, or in the midst of the two thieves, or in the midst of Moses and Elijah conversing with him on the mountain? is taken from book 18 of The City of God, chapter 32. From there too the Sibylline verses in ch. 23 were transferred here. With Gregory, homily 33 on the Gospels, the preacher uses this at the opening of the sermon: Since it is more fitting to weep than to say anything. And likewise ch. 17 has certain other things in agreement with homily 10 of the same [Gregory] on the Gospels. In ch. 15 he says that the poet Virgil, by that verse,
now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven,

bore witness to Christ: which Augustine, in letter 104 to Nectarius, n. 11, far more truly calls a flattering poem, addressed to a nobleman, namely Pollio. Bernard Vinding in his Critica Augustiniana points out the barbarism of the diction, and censures some things as inept; but these were faults of the editions, corrected here from the Remigian codex eight hundred years old, in which it is entitled Sermon of Saint Augustine on the Creed; from three Vatican [manuscripts], from one of Beauvais, of the abbey of St Quentin, from the Corbie [manuscript], etc.
